page.title: Creative Operations Workflow Guide
page.description: Learn the seven stages, tools, roles, timelines and metrics that define a repeatable creative operations workflow.
page.h1: What does a creative operations workflow look like?
page.definition: Creative operations workflow is a structured sequence of seven stages — intake, brief, production, review, approval, publishing and reporting — each with a single owner and a defined output, supported by work‑management, review and publishing tools.
page.quick_answer: Map the seven stages to owners, assign a tool for each hand‑off, and set a review gate so every asset moves from brief to publish in five to ten working days.

sections.h2: What are the seven stages of a creative operations workflow?

blocks.p: The workflow moves through intake, brief, production, review, approval, publishing and reporting, each owned by one person and producing a concrete deliverable.

ul: Intake – capture request and assign owner
Brief – document goals, audience and specs

blocks.p: Work‑management platforms handle intake and scheduling, collaborative docs capture briefs, review tools manage feedback, and publishing platforms push final assets.

ul: Asana, Monday.com or Airtable for calendar and task tracking
Google Docs or Notion for brief creation
Frame.io for video review, Figma for design review
Bynder or Brandfolder for asset storage
WordPress, Webflow or HubSpot for publishing

sections.h2: How long does a typical content cycle take?

blocks.p: A long‑form article usually moves from approved brief to publish in five to ten working days, with most time spent in review and approval cycles.

sections.h2: What roles make up a creative ops team?

blocks.p: A full team includes a producer, project manager, designer, copywriter and analyst, though small groups combine several roles in one person.

sections.h2: How do you measure workflow performance?

blocks.p: Track cycle time, revision rounds, on‑time rate and capacity use to see bottlenecks and improve throughput.

ul: Cycle time – days from brief to publish
Revision rounds – number of feedback loops per asset
On‑time rate – percentage of deliverables met deadline
Capacity use – workload balance across team members

faq.q: How do I assign owners to each stage?
faq.a: Create a responsibility matrix that lists every stage, names a single owner, and defines the hand‑off criteria; review it in the kickoff meeting so everyone knows when to act.

faq.q: What tool stack works for a small team?
faq.a: Combine a lightweight task board such as Asana with Google Docs for briefs, Figma for design review, and HubSpot for publishing and analytics; this covers intake through reporting without extra licences.

faq.q: When should I add a review gate?
faq.a: Insert a gate after production and before approval; require at least two stakeholders to sign off so errors are caught early and the approval stage stays fast.
